title: Methods
summary: Give a piece of code a name, hand it inputs, and get a result back.

steps.title: Name it once, use it anywhere
body: You have been *calling* methods since your first line: `Console.WriteLine(...)`, `int.Parse(...)`. Now you will write your own.
A **method** is a named block of code. You define it once and run it as often as you like by calling its name.
- `void` means the method gives nothing back. It just does something.
- `Cheer` is its name. Method names start with a capital letter by convention.
- The braces hold the **body**: the code that runs on each call.
- `Cheer();` is a **call**. Defining a method runs nothing. Only calls do.
Why bother? Without methods you copy and paste. Then you find a bug and have to fix it in every copy.

steps.prompt: Arrange the lines to **define** a method `Knock` first, and then **call** it twice.
steps.explain: The header comes first, then the body in braces, then the calls. C# does not mind whether the definition sits above or below the calls, as long as it is complete.

steps.title: Inputs and outputs
body: A method that always does the same thing is not very useful. **Parameters** let the caller pass values in. A **return value** passes a result back.
- `int` in front of the name is the **return type**: the type of the value handed back.
- `int a, int b` are the **parameters**: variables that exist only inside the method.
- `2` and `3` in the call are the **arguments**. They are copied into `a` and `b`, in order.
- `return` ends the method **immediately** and hands its value to the caller.
A call to a method that returns a value *is* a value. You can store it, print it, or use it in a bigger expression: `Add(1, 2) * 10`.

prompt: Match each piece of this program to its name.
pairs: hands the result back to the caller

steps.explain: `Twice(3)` returns 6, so `x` is 6. Then `Twice(6)` returns 12, and 12 + 1 is 13.

steps.title: The larger one
prompt: Write a method `int Max(int a, int b)` that returns the larger of its two arguments. If they are equal, return either.
`Max(3, 7)` returns `7`. Do it yourself: `Math.Max` is off limits here.
starter: // return the larger of a and b
hints: `return` ends the method on the spot, so `if (a > b) return a;` followed by `return b;` covers both cases.
A ternary does it in one line: `return a > b ? a : b;`

steps.title: One-line methods
body: Many methods are a single `return`. For those, C# has a shorter form using `=>`, called an **expression-bodied** method.
No braces and no `return`: the value of the expression after `=>` *is* the result. It works for `void` methods too:
Use it when the body is one short expression. If you need an `if` or a loop, use braces.

steps.prompt: Complete the one-line method so `IsEven(4)` returns `true` and `IsEven(7)` returns `false`.
steps.explain: A comparison produces a `bool`, so that is the return type. `=>` replaces both the braces and the word `return`.

steps.title: Scope: what lives where
body: A variable exists only inside the block where it is declared. That region is its **scope**.
Console.WriteLine(result);      // error: result does not exist here
`w`, `h` and `result` are created when `Area` is called and thrown away when it returns. The only thing that gets out is the returned value.
Parameters receive a **copy** of the argument. Changing a parameter inside the method does not touch the caller's variable.
This is a feature. A method that depends only on its parameters can be read, tested and reused on its own, without knowing anything about the rest of the program.

steps.explain: `n` is a copy of `score`. The method changes and prints its own copy (15). The caller's `score` is still 5.

steps.prompt: `AddTen` above cannot change the caller's `score`. What is the normal way to get the new value out of a method?
options: Make the method `return` the new value, and store it: `score = AddTen(score);`
Give the parameter the same name as the caller's variable
Print the new value inside the method
steps.explain: Values go in through parameters and come out through `return`. A parameter is a copy whatever it is called, and printing a value shows it to the user without giving it to the caller.

steps.title: Vowel counter
prompt: Write two methods. The second should **call** the first.
- `bool IsVowel(char c)` returns `true` when `c` is one of `a`, `e`, `i`, `o`, `u`. Lowercase letters only.
- `int CountVowels(string text)` returns how many characters of `text` are vowels.
starter: // true for a, e, i, o, u
// look at every char of text and ask IsVowel about it
solution: bool IsVowel(char c) => c == 'a' || c == 'e' || c == 'i' || c == 'o' || c == 'u';
hints: `IsVowel` is one long condition: `c == 'a' || c == 'e' || ...`. Remember a `char` uses single quotes.
In `CountVowels`, start a counter at 0 and walk the string with `foreach (char c in text)`.
Inside the loop: `if (IsVowel(c)) count++;`. After the loop: `return count;`.
